newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans watch rebels tighten grip on eastern town.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans watch rebels tighten grip on eastern town.

text.p: Residents of the east Zairean town of Bukavu watched cautiously on Saturday as anti-government rebels strengthened their grip.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Friday appointed a governor of the Bukavu area seized by rebels late last month.
The new governor, Cubaka Anatole Bishikwabo, is a member of the local Bashi tribe and his deputy is a Banyamulenge, the ethnic Tutsis who launched the rebellion, rebel sources said in Nairobi.

It was unclear if Bishikwabo was appointed to head the existing province of South Kivu, whose capital is Bukavu, or a brand-new entity. But Kabila and other rebel leaders have made clear they are not seceding from Zaire.
Bukavu, situated right on the border with Rwanda, appeared unfazed by the change in its administration.
Shops in Bukavu, whose mansions overlook beautiful Lake Kivu, were open as usual and residents lazily walked along the streets or stopped to chat to one another.
Residents said there were no major shortages in town apart from kerosene which is brought in bright yellow jerry cans from nearby Rwanda.

The only sign of rebel fighters in town were three teenage youths armed with automatic rifles and proudly displaying hand grenades hanging on their belts. They were guarding a compound of government offices.
"Most people have nothing against the rebels," said Paskal, a young man who recently switched from performing traditional witch-craft to working as a paramedic in a local hospital.
"In terms of democracy there could hardly be any change for the worse after government rule," he added.
Like the rest of Zaire, Bukavu was under President Mobutu Sese Seko's autocratic rule for 31 years before government troops were routed by the rebels.
"But they (rebels) are newcomers here and they still have to prove that they are serious. If they try to replace one oppression with another, people will simply not accept them," Paskal said.
Beneath the sleepy, relaxed mood the rebels' grip on the town was tight.
A European missionary who declined to be identified said he had to seek permission from the new authorities for every trip to visit congregations outside Bukavu.
Paskal and other residents of the town refused to elaborate on the shaky issue of hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees stranded in eastern Zaire by the recent fighting.
Kabila's fighters have struck at Hutu militants who controlled refugee camps both north and south of Bukavu, prompting an exodus of around 500,000 refugees back to Rwanda last week.
But some observers say attacks on the militants near Bukavu led to many civilian casualties.
"Some of the refugees were killed by Kabila's people, others fled elsewhere," a Bukavu resident said.
The rebels say most refugees have already left for Rwanda while relief workers believe up to 700,000 are still in Zaire.
"We believe there are more than 670,000 refugees in that area (east Zaire)," said Mans Nyberg, a coordinator for the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR).
Nyberg is stranded together with dozens of other relief workers on the Rwandan side of the border with Zaire.
"We are here with an investigation team which is ready to go and assess the size of needed help. But they (rebels) would not let us go," he said.
The rebels have allowed journalists to visit Zaire but a group of rebel guards, extravagantly dressed in green and yellow overcoats, are blocking the entry of relief workers.
